Rumors about Apple developing a foldable clamshell device have been around for a long time. Some say it's an iPad, a Mac, both, or a hybrid of the two.

A recent report suggests that while this project was once a priority for new CEO John Ternus, the plan has been cancelled — but I don't think that description is entirely accurate...

Personally, I think the concept of a Mac and iPad hybrid is essentially obsolete. Today's Macs can run iPhone and iPad apps, and for many users, iPhone Mirroring achieves the same result. We are also seeing an increasingly obvious convergence between the two operating systems, and I believe this trend will continue: Apple's old argument of "we won't merge the refrigerator and the toaster" is long out of date.

That said, I do believe that once the technology matures enough for a soft keyboard to replace a traditional hard one, we will eventually see an all-screen foldable Mac. This won't happen in the short term, but it will happen one day.

Mid-stage: The dynamic keyboard

I think we are still far from that day, because I believe there will be a transitional stage featuring a dynamic hardware keyboard first. I discussed nearly a decade ago why I thought this was the future trend. Although such technology is in use today in niche areas, it has yet to enter the mainstream.

The Sonder Keyboard was one of the early attempts, using tiny e-ink displays to redefine key labels and functions.

For example, for someone who spends the whole day editing in Final Cut Pro, a traditional QWERTY keyboard is almost useless — which precisely explains why physical keyboards and keyboard covers have a market.

Wouldn't it be much smarter if our MacBook keyboards, or the desktop Magic Keyboard, could automatically adjust key labels according to the application in use?

Soft keyboard that feels like a hard one

But the longer-term goal has always been a completely soft keyboard. Back in 2016, I pointed out that Steve Jobs' argument for virtual keys on the smartphone when he introduced the iPhone applies equally to the Mac keyboard.

Of course, soft keyboards have three major problems:

  • Glass keyboards are not comfortable to type on
  • We rely on key travel for feedback and comfort
  • Touch typists need to feel the keys before pressing them

Apple has filed patents for each of these three challenges. First, using a flexible display rather than traditional glass allows the surface to deform when virtual keys are pressed. The second problem can be solved by combining such deformation with haptic motors. Finally, regarding the ability to feel physical keys with the fingers, there are two solutions.

Apple's patent uses electrostatic charges to create surface texture changes for tactile feedback. In other words, even if the surface remains flat, applying charges to the display surface can make the user feel the presence of physical keys. And in 2023, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University proposed another approach.

It's only a question of "when," not "if"

Of course, these technologies are still at a very early stage, but we only need to look at the development of the Mac trackpad to know it's not impossible. Trackpads still sound and feel like mechanical devices, but in reality they have been solid-state devices using haptic feedback to simulate physical clicks for years — and the effect is extremely convincing.

Soft keyboards will eventually reach the same level of maturity. Whether using Apple's currently proposed approach or technologies not yet seen, all three problems will be solved.

When that happens, Steve's argument applies equally to the Mac. Operating in clamshell form, the keyboard will take on the most appropriate shape for the task at hand. When we only need one large screen — whether for watching movies or drawing with Apple Pencil — we simply unfold the device to get double the display area.

So I fully agree that the first-generation product may be put on hold for now, but that absolutely does not mean the plan has been cancelled. This technology will eventually come to fruition.

Those are my thoughts — what do you think? Feel free to share in the comments.
